opening.headline: Move beyond the structure of directly calling model APIs for each service, and understand the role of an AI gateway that consolidates routing, filtering, and usage tracking at a single point.
body: Imagine an organization where services A, B, and C each hold their own keys and directly call the model API. You'd need to separately verify how much each service is using the model, sensitive information could inadvertently leak into prompts with no way to block it, and if you wanted to change the model or tool, you'd have to modify the code for each service individually.

In this class, we examine the gateway that consolidates control from three perspectives: the gateway components acting as an entry and exit point for agent traffic, content filters attached to the gateway and their deployment sequence, and routing and expenditure limits for model requests. Finally, we explain in two stages a case where service keys are aggregated to the gateway.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: The gateway's responsibilities—routing, filtering, and usage logging—can be explained.
The control points before and after introducing the gateway can be distinguished.

screens.title: Each service directly calls the model.
screens.lead: First, take a look at a structure without a gateway. Think about where you should be looking each time control is needed.

visual.alt: This is a tangled structure where each service holds its own key and directly calls two model providers.
labels: Capacity should be verified separately by service.

paragraphs: Service A, B, and C obtain API keys from their respective model providers. No team did anything wrong. It was simply the fastest way to add required functionality.

However, when looking at the organization as a whole, four issues arise. It must be verified separately by service whether a certain model has been used. Sensitive information mixed into prompts can escape externally, with no point in the middle to block it. To switch models or tools, the code must be modified for each service. Furthermore, keys are dispersed across services, making it difficult to trace where a leak occurs.

The commonality is that the points of control are scattered throughout the service. To consolidate control into a single location, there must be a point where all calls between the service and the model pass through. This point is the gateway.
The question to be answered in this class is this: Where should what be placed in order to consolidate control into one location?

callout.label: Things to think about
callout.text: A single control point is an advantage, yet it also represents a single point of failure. Pay close attention to how this balance is addressed in this course.

screens.outro: First, let's consider in your organization what the call path looks like.

screens.title: Recall the model invocation path of our service
screens.lead: When you select each question, the instructor's thoughts unfold. You won't have to enter or submit your answer, so think about it in your head first and then press it.

items.prompt: If multiple services are directly calling the model API, where are the keys stored?
items.answer: In a structure where services directly make calls, keys are scattered across environment variables or secret stores for each service. The more keys there are, the harder it becomes to rotate and replace them, and copies of the keys may end up on developers' notebooks. Using a gateway consolidates upper-level credentials at the gateway, and developers simply use company login credentials instead of keys.

items.prompt: Where are usage records stored, and can they be viewed at once?
items.answer: Since each provider and each key is separately aggregated, combining data is necessary to view corporate-wide status. It is often difficult to distinguish how much each service or team has used. When a call passes through a point, it can record entries in the same format at that point.

items.prompt: Is there a point that checks the call content?
items.answer: If the service is directly invoked, the check must be handled by the service's code. Since each service has a different implementation level, it's difficult to apply consistent standards. However, by attaching a filter to the gateway, the same check can be applied to all calls.

screens.outro: Let's start by examining the agent traffic gateway, the entry and exit point of the gateway's first component.

screens.title: Agent Gateway: Entry and exit point for agent traffic
screens.lead: When you select a number marker in the configuration, you can see in detail the role of each component. Keep in mind that all connections pass through the gateway, and verify them in sequence accordingly.

visual.alt: User, agent, tool flows through the Agent Gateway, while identity, list, policy, and observation components form the surrounding architecture around the gateway.
labels: All entry and exit points of connections

markers.label: Entrance/Exit
markers.title: Agent Gateway is the entry and exit point for all connections.
markers.body: The Agent Gateway is a core component of the Agent Platform, serving as the network entry point for all interactions involving agents. Connections between users and agents, agents and tools, and agents themselves all pass through this gateway. Therefore, security administrators can protect all connections from a single point.

markers.label: Identity
markers.title: Agent Identity: Unique ID for each agent
markers.body: Each agent is assigned a unique and secure ID. This ID is used for authentication, access control, and auditing, much like a digital signature of the agent. The agent's identity is protected by context-aware access using mTLS and DPoP. The caller's identity is determined based on the agent's identity rather than its self-declaration.

markers.label: Approval list
markers.title: Agent Registry: Central list of approved targets
markers.body: Agent Registry is the central directory of approved agents, tools, MCP servers, and endpoints within an organization. Gateways verify permissions against this list before allowing connections. Departments must have their tools listed in order to be connected, thereby structurally preventing tools from proliferating independently across departments.

markers.label: Access policy
markers.title: IAM Unified Access Policy: Block unless explicitly allowed
markers.body: Access policies link an agent's identity to approved tools and endpoints registered in the Agent Registry. By default, all connections are blocked and only allowed when explicit IAM policies permit them. Because it operates on an allowlist basis, new connections must be reviewed and approved before they are enabled.

markers.label: Connection handling
markers.title: Protocol conversion and encryption connection
markers.body: The gateway handles protocol translation between agents and tools, supporting protocols such as MCP, REST, and gRPC. The connection segment is encrypted using mTLS. Since each service does not need to independently implement its own protocol and encryption, all calls are subject to the same level of protection.

markers.label: Observation
markers.title: Observation data generated at the network layer
markers.body: All interaction observation data is generated at the network layer and delivered to Agent Observability, not from the service code. This means that logs are not lost even if the service forgets to write them. This is why usage and call records can be viewed in one place.

screens.outro: We will continue to examine the content filter attached to entry points and its implementation method.

screens.title: Filter and Usage Tracking Point: Model Armor
screens.lead: Switch between the two states to compare how the Model Armor template can be used in different modes. The two modes are also related to the order of introduction.

states.label: Audit & Log Mode
states.body:
Model Armor is a content security filter that attaches to the gateway and performs real-time inspection of user prompts and tool responses. It detects risks such as prompt injection, escape attempts, exposure of harmful content, and disclosure of sensitive information.

In inspection and logging mode, Model Armor does not block content but detects and logs violations. The logs appear in the Model Armor page of the Google Cloud Console and are also visible in Security Command Center. This mode is appropriate for understanding the volume of traffic and how long it takes to process according to rules, as well as for assessing whether normal operations are being incorrectly flagged.

states.label: Block/Obstruct Mode
states.body:
Setting the same template to block and hide modes prevents policy violations or obscures sensitive content. By filtering violations before they reach the model, or before responses are delivered to users, this step reduces actual risks.

However, directly enabling block mode for rules that may contain false positives can disrupt normal operations. Therefore, first evaluate and log in inspection mode, then gradually enable block and hide modes only for rules that are confirmed safe. There are also constraints to consider: the regions used by the template must match those of the integrated services, and inline ingress protection is limited to the ADK agent. These limitations do not apply to the entire Model Armor system, as egress protection also includes MCP servers, OpenAI-style services, and A2A traffic.

screens.outro: If a filter examines the content, routing determines where the request is sent.

screens.title: Multi-model routing and inference gateway
screens.lead: Select each tab to compare how two different types of gateways handle routing. Pay attention to the fact that the two gateways have different issues when it comes to fullness.

tabs.label: Claude apps gateway
tabs.body:
The Claude Apps Gateway is an on-premises service that sits between the developer's Claude Code client and the model provider. Instead of using API keys or cloud credentials, developers log in through their organization's Identity Provider (IdP). The gateway stores the top-level credentials.

The gateway applies model access and management settings based on IdP groups and forwards usage telemetry to the organization's own observability stack. It is suitable for organizations that must route inference through a cloud provider or have data residency requirements. Rather than managing keys, storing top-level credentials has become the gateway's new core responsibility.

tabs.label: Inference Gateway
tabs.body:
Kubernetes' Gateway API Inference Extension is an official project designed to optimize routing when hosting generative models directly within Kubernetes. If existing gateways support extension processing protocols, they can be transformed into inference gateways, including Envoy Gateway, kgateway, and GKE Gateway.

Here, the router is structured as a combination of a proxy with an Endpoint Picker. For each request, it evaluates metrics and capabilities of individual endpoints—such as prefix cache status or LoRA adapter availability—and selects the most appropriate endpoint. This routing approach optimizes performance and availability for organizations that host model services directly rather than relying on third-party services.

tabs.label: Compare
tabs.body:
The two gateways address different issues. The Claude Apps Gateway is more concerned with who accesses which model, where credentials are stored, and how costs are recorded. In contrast, the Inference Gateway provides performance-driven routing, determining which endpoint within directly hosted models to send requests to.

Additionally, the Inference Gateway can be used in conjunction with upper-level AI gateway products. By placing self-hosted models side by side behind upper-level gateway services—such as a model service provider—the caller sees only a single path. This is an example of multi-model routing.

screens.outro: Next, I will verify the settings that extend from usage logging to quota control, in code.

screens.title: From usage tracking to expenditure limit
screens.lead: The following is a command to exceed the spending limit using the management API of the Claude Apps Gateway. Check the meaning for each line number in the right-hand description, and review what symptoms appear when configurations are misaligned.

data.code:
#Organization-wide default: $500 per developer per month (50,000 cents)
curl -sS https://claude-gateway.internal.example.com/v1/organizations/spend_limits \
  -H "x-api-key: $GATEWAY_ADMIN_WRITE_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"scope": {"type": "organization"}, "amount": "50000", "period": "monthly"}'

#The contractors group is stricter: $100 per person per day (1,000 cents)
curl -sS https://claude-gateway.internal.example.com/v1/organizations/spend_limits \
  -H "x-api-key: $GATEWAY_ADMIN_WRITE_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"scope": {"type": "rbac_group", "rbac_group_id": "contractors"}, "amount": "10000", "period": "daily"}'

#When the limit is exceeded, the following request is rejected with status 429 and is blocked until the period expires.

notes.note: This is the basic limit for the entire organization. If scope.type is organization, this value applies to all developers, and amount is an integer string in US dollars and cents. If you mistakenly interpret the value as dollars and enter 500, a $5 limit is applied, immediately blocking normal operations.

An example of overlapping stricter limits at the group level. rbac_group refers to the IdP group name, and the group limit is per member rather than a shared pool. If the group name differs from the IdP name, the limit will not be applied to the intended users.

If the request limit is exceeded, the gateway returns 429 and blocks further requests until the period expires or the administrator increases the limit. The limit is set via the management API, not in the gateway.yaml file; therefore, be careful not to get confused by assuming that changing the configuration file alone will resolve limit issues.

screens.outro: Now let's move on to an explanation of applying these elements to real-world cases.

screens.title: Explanation: Aggregate service keys to the gateway (1) Create an entrance
screens.lead: The instructor divides the process of gathering scattered keys by service and consolidating them at the gateway into two parts. First, they follow the initial four steps of establishing the entrance. Selecting the right arrow proceeds to the next step.

visual.alt: Before-and-after comparison diagram showing the transition from a structure where five services directly called each other to a structure where they call through a gateway.

steps.title: Step 1: Create a table to represent the current status
steps.body: Assume that five services call two model providers using different keys each. Create a table listing the services, the providers being called, the location where the keys are stored, the call volume, and the responsible personnel. This table serves as an indicator showing where control points are dispersed and confirms whether direct calls have been eliminated after the introduction of the gateway.

steps.title: Step 2: Place the gateway at the entrance and switch the key.
steps.body: Place a gateway between the service and the model provider, and move the storage of upper-level authentication credentials to the gateway. Now the keys are not stored within the service but rather at a single gateway location. The key management responsibility does not disappear—it simply concentrates at the gateway. Therefore, the secret management and access control of the gateway become the new core responsibilities.

steps.title: Step 3: The service connects using internal login.
steps.body: Services and developers log in to the gateway via the company's Identity Provider (IdP) instead of using API keys. This links who made the call to corporate identity. Access for former employees or those who have moved is simply revoked by updating the IdP assignment, eliminating the need to physically retrieve or recover keys.

steps.title: Step 4: Define an accessible model using group settings
steps.body: Models available to each service and team are defined at the IdP group level. For example, only low-cost models are allowed for experimental service groups, while only approved models are permitted for operational service groups. One advantage of routing controls is the ability to change model access via gateway settings without modifying service codes.

screens.outro: Since the entrance has been established, we will now proceed to examine the backend section, where we increase the filter and limit settings and verify whether direct calls are present.

screens.title: Explanation: Aggregate service keys to the gateway (2) Filters and limits
screens.lead: This is the second part of the explanation. Follow the sequence in which the gateway is installed, filters and limits are applied. Pay attention to the reason for maintaining this order.

steps.title: Step 5: Attach the Model Armor in inspection and logging mode
steps.body: Initially, attach the Model Armor template in inspection and logging mode. Since no restrictions are currently in place, this will have no impact on services. Over several days, collect logs to observe how long specific rules take to apply and to assess the scale of normal operations being mistakenly interrupted. Skipping this phase and immediately enabling blocking could result in unexpected service disruptions.

steps.title: Step 6: Starts with valid rules and blocks or obscures them.
steps.body: Review the records and enable rules without false positives first, then move to blocking and filtering modes. For example, rules involving sensitive data exposure—where violations are clearly defined—should be prioritized as candidates. Rules that still produce false positives should be adjusted and then re-verified in record mode. This approach ensures the filter's effectiveness while avoiding service disruptions.

steps.title: Step 7: Set an expenditure limit and define actions that exceed it.
steps.body: Daily, weekly, and monthly spending limits are set per user, RBAC group, and organizational scope. Group and organizational settings establish per-user baseline limits, not shared spending pools. If limits are exceeded, the gateway returns a 429 error and blocks further requests until the period expires or an administrator increases the limit, thus requiring pre-configuration of how the service should behave when limits are reached. These limits act as circuit breakers to prevent a single, overactive agent from consuming the entire organization's agreement under a shared identity setup where all calls originate from a single shared credential.

steps.title: Step 8: Verify that no direct call path remains.
steps.body: Finally, compare the table created in stage 1 to verify whether any calls bypass the gateway. If any service is directly calling using the old key, then that call exists outside of the filter, limits, and logging. You must jointly review the network policy to retire the old key and block direct calls so that the gateway becomes a single point of control.

screens.outro: We will consolidate and summarize the conclusion of the case on a single screen.

screens.title: The gateway is a single point of control.
screens.lead: We summarize the content presented so far from the perspective of control points before and after implementation.

paragraphs: Before introduction, key management, usage logging, prompt validation, and model selection were scattered across various services. After introduction, all calls pass through the gateway, enabling these four functions to be uniformly applied along the journey path. The service handles only the call itself, while identity, policy, filtering, and logging are managed by the gateway.

The gateway's role can be summarized in three aspects. Routing involves forwarding requests to the appropriate model or endpoint based on identity, policy, and metrics. Filtering entails inspecting prompts and responses to prevent injection attacks and sensitive information leaks. Usage logging records calls in the same format at the network layer and enforces upper limits on consumption.

There are principles governing the introduction order. Filters begin with inspection and logging, then proceed to blocking upon observing impact. Access policies start with a default of denying unless explicitly allowed. Spending limits are set as circuit breakers to ensure that a single surge of calls does not affect the entire organization.

Finally, it's important to remember the limitations of gateways. The keys are not being lost but rather converging through the gateway, so the storage and access control of these keys become new core responsibilities. If direct calls bypassing the gateway remain, the advantage of having a single point of entry is lost; therefore, after deployment, it's essential to verify that there are no direct call paths.

We have summarized three key questions to evaluate the feasibility of our introduction plan. Are all services calling through the gateway? Does the gateway's access policy start with the default of denying everything unless explicitly allowed? Are filters and spending limits being applied in an order that does not impact service functionality? Once we can answer these questions, we can determine where to place the gateway within our organization's call flow and what to control first. For example, moving the gateway to services with the highest call volume yields significant benefits but also carries substantial impact; alternatively, we can begin by validating the order starting with services that have minimal impact. Documenting these checks at the initial implementation stage enables us to apply the same criteria when adding new services in the future.

callout.label: something to remember
callout.text: The gateway is a single point of control. It aggregates routing, filtering, and usage logging into one location, starting with inspection and logging, and escalating to blocking.

checks.intro: Check for yourself what you just learned. Results are not recorded.
checks.q: A new agent attempts to connect to a tool that is not approved. What is the default behavior of the Agent Gateway?
options: Connects if not explicitly allowed in IAM policies
Only retain the observation data and temporarily allow the connection to pass through.
The agent trusts the permissions it has declared on its own.
Model Armor does not decide before viewing the response.
checks.explain: The IAM unified access policy blocks any connection not explicitly allowed by default, and this is supported by the approval list in the Agent Registry and the Agent Identity.

wrong.1: Observation is conducted separately, and unauthorized connections are inherently blocked.
wrong.2: The agent trusts neither its own unique ID nor its policy for self-declaration.
wrong.3: Access policies are applied during the connection stage, independently of response inspection.

checks.correctFeedback: Yes. It is blocked by default unless explicitly allowed.
checks.incorrectFeedback: Think again. Consider whether the default value for access policies is allow or deny.

checks.intro: Check for yourself what you just learned. Results are not recorded.
checks.q: A user has exceeded their daily spending limit assigned to them in the Claude Apps Gateway. What happens now?
options: The excess in the next month's invoice will be settled at once.
Requests become slower but the calls themselves are still processed.
Allowed until the gateway.yaml is reloaded
429 is returned and the restriction is lifted either when the period ends or until the administrator uploads.
checks.explain: Quotas are enforced per developer, group, or organization on a daily, weekly, or monthly basis, and exceedances are blocked with error 429. This prevents agents from consuming all the organization's allocated resources and causing overload.

wrong.0: It is not settlement but blocked at the excess point.
wrong.1: Instead of reducing speed, it blocks the request.
wrong.2: The limit is set via the management API, not gateway.yaml.

checks.correctFeedback: Correct. Requests are blocked with status 429 when the limit is exceeded.
checks.incorrectFeedback: Sorry. When you exceed the limit, recall the response returned by the gateway and the duration of the delay.

checks.explain: The filter begins with inspection and logging, proceeds safely through blocking, and finally verifies at the end that there is no direct call path bypassing limits after the threshold is reached.

glossary.def: A network gateway that applies identity, policy, and filtering to all agent connections passing through it.
This involves sending a request to the appropriate model or endpoint based on identity, policy, metric, or cost.
This configuration routes requests for models hosted directly in Kubernetes through a proxy and Endpoint Picker to the optimal endpoint.
A content security filter attached to the gateway that checks for prompt injection and sensitive information leakage.
Developer, group, or organizational unit-level settings that impose limits on usage per day, week, or month; requests are rejected if these limits are exceeded.

misconceptions.myth: The gateway is simply a proxy that forwards requests only.
misconceptions.fact: The gateway is a centralized control point that applies authentication, access policies, content filtering, and monitoring.

misconceptions.myth: With a gateway, key management is no longer required.
misconceptions.fact: The key will be removed from the service and will reside in the gateway. The storage and access control of the key will become the new core responsibility.

misconceptions.myth: Filters should be turned on in blocking mode from the start for maximum safety.
misconceptions.fact: If there is an anomaly, normal operations are disrupted. After observing the impact through inspection and records, rules that do not pose a problem are gradually blocked.

closing.lead: Summarizes what was covered in this class.
points: The gateway is a single point of control that consolidates routing, filtering, and usage logging.
Before introduction, control points were scattered across services; after introduction, they are uniformly applied along the fuel path.
Filtering starts with inspection and recording, then proceeds to blocking in a safe order.
The expenditure limit acts as a circuit breaker to prevent the overflow of shared credentials.
